title: Libraries and Paper in the Abbasid Age
summary: How papermaking reached Baghdad in the Abbasid age, made books cheaper, filled book markets and libraries such as the House of Wisdom, and helped scholars translate and share knowledge.
poll: Paper was one of the most important inventions in history.

versions.title: Books for All
versions.text:
Long ago, a great town stood by a river. It was Baghdad. Its rulers loved books.

At first, books were hard to make. Some were made on skin. Skin cost a lot. So there were not many books.

Then a new thing came. It was paper! Paper first came from China. Then the skill went west. In the late 700s, they made their own paper.

How was it made? Men took old cloth. They beat it to a soft mush. They spread it thin on a screen. Then they let it dry.

Paper did not cost much. So more books were made. One street sold them.

The town had a big library. It was the House of Wisdom. Wise men came to it. They were scholars. They read and wrote. They would translate books. They put the words in Arabic.

They read on math, stars, and health. They shared what they learned.

In time, paper went to Spain. Then it went all over the world. Now we use it each day!

versions.title: Libraries and Paper in the Abbasid Age
versions.text:
More than a thousand years ago, Baghdad was one of the largest and richest cities in the world. It stood beside the Tigris River, and its rulers, the Abbasids, valued books and learning.

Before paper arrived, books were hard and costly to make. Many were written on parchment, a material made from animal skin. Because parchment was expensive, books were rare, and only rich families could afford them.

Paper changed this situation. It was first made in China, and the skill of making it gradually spread west, so that by the late 700s, Baghdad had its own paper mills.

To make paper, workers soaked old linen rags and beat them into a soft, wet pulp. They spread the pulp thinly on a screen, let it dry, and then polished the sheets until they were smooth enough for ink.

Because paper was much cheaper than parchment, people could make far more books. Copyists wrote out each manuscript by hand, and a whole market in Baghdad was filled with book sellers and their buyers.

In that busy market, readers met to talk about new books, compare copies, and argue about ideas, much as people today gather in a bookshop or library.

The city also had a famous library known as the House of Wisdom, where scholars from many lands gathered to study. They would translate books from Greek, Persian, and other languages into Arabic.

These scholars studied math, astronomy, and medicine, and they wrote new books that shared their discoveries.

Over time, papermaking spread to Spain and then across Europe, and today people around the world use paper every day.

versions.title: Libraries and Paper in the Abbasid Age
versions.text:
More than a thousand years ago, Baghdad was one of the largest and wealthiest cities in the world. It stood beside the Tigris River, and its rulers, the Abbasids, considered books and learning very valuable.

Before paper arrived, books were difficult and costly to produce. Many were written on parchment, a material made from animal skin. Because parchment was expensive, books were rare, and only wealthy families could afford them.

Paper transformed this situation. It was invented in China, and the technique of making it gradually spread west across Asia, so that by the late 700s, Baghdad had its own paper mills.

To make paper, workers soaked old linen rags and beat them into a soft, wet pulp. They spread the pulp thinly on a screen, allowed it to dry, and then polished the sheets until they were smooth enough for ink.

Because paper was much cheaper than parchment, people could produce far more books. Copyists wrote out each manuscript by hand, and a whole market in Baghdad was filled with booksellers and their customers.

In that busy market, readers gathered to discuss new books, compare different copies, and debate ideas, much as people today meet in a bookshop or library.

The city also had a famous library known as the House of Wisdom, where scholars from many regions gathered to study. They would translate books from Greek, Persian, and other languages into Arabic, so that old ideas could be read by new students.

These scholars studied mathematics, astronomy, and medicine, and they wrote original books that shared their discoveries.

Eventually, papermaking spread to Spain and then across Europe, and today people around the world use paper every day.

versions.title: Libraries and Paper in the Abbasid Age
versions.text:
More than a thousand years ago, Baghdad was one of the largest and wealthiest cities in the world. It stood beside the Tigris River, and its rulers, the Abbasid caliphs, considered books and learning extremely valuable.

Before paper arrived, books were difficult and costly to produce. Many were written on parchment, a material prepared from animal skin, or on papyrus imported from Egypt. Because these materials were expensive, books were rare, and only wealthy families could afford them.

Paper transformed this situation. It was invented in China, and the technique of making it gradually spread west across Central Asia, so that by the late 700s, Baghdad had established its own paper mills.

To manufacture paper, workers soaked old linen rags and other plant fibers, then beat them into a soft, wet pulp. They spread the pulp thinly on a screen, allowed it to dry, and polished the sheets until they were smooth enough for ink.

Because paper was considerably cheaper than parchment, people could produce far more books. Copyists wrote out each manuscript by hand, and an entire market in Baghdad, crowded with the shops of booksellers and stationers, became a lively meeting place where readers examined new titles and debated ideas.

These booksellers were known as warraqs, a title that comes from waraq, the Arabic word for paper, and many of them were scholars who copied, edited, and sold manuscripts.

The city also possessed a celebrated library known as the House of Wisdom. It flourished as scholars from many regions gathered to study, and they would translate books from Greek, Persian, and Indian languages into Arabic, which preserved ancient knowledge that might otherwise have been lost.

These scholars investigated mathematics, astronomy, and medicine. They composed original books that communicated their discoveries. One of them, the mathematician al-Khwarizmi, wrote a famous book about solving equations, and the word algebra comes from its Arabic title.

Eventually, papermaking spread to Spain and then across Europe, and today people around the world use paper every day, often without realizing how much they owe to the papermakers and scholars of Baghdad.

versions.title: Libraries and Paper in the Abbasid Age
versions.text:
More than a thousand years ago, Baghdad was one of the largest and wealthiest cities in the world. It stood beside the Tigris River, and its rulers, the Abbasid caliphs, considered books and scholarship extraordinarily valuable.

Before paper arrived, books were difficult and costly to produce, since many were written on parchment, a material prepared from animal skin, or on papyrus imported from Egypt. Because these materials were expensive, manuscripts were scarce, and only wealthy families could afford them.

Paper transformed this situation dramatically: it was originally invented in China, and the technique of manufacturing it gradually spread westward across Central Asia, so that by the late 700s, Baghdad had established its own paper mills.

To manufacture paper, workers soaked discarded linen rags and other plant fibers, then beat them into a soft, wet pulp. They distributed the pulp thinly across a screen, allowed it to dry, and polished the sheets until they were sufficiently smooth for ink.

Because paper was considerably cheaper than parchment, people could produce far more books, and professional copyists reproduced each manuscript by hand, and an entire market in Baghdad, crowded with the shops of booksellers and stationers, became an energetic meeting place where readers examined new titles and debated ideas.

These booksellers were known as warraqs, a professional title derived from waraq, the Arabic word for paper, and numerous warraqs were themselves accomplished intellectuals who meticulously copied, corrected, and distributed manuscripts throughout the community, contributing significantly to the circulation of knowledge.

The city also possessed a celebrated library known as the House of Wisdom, which flourished as scholars from numerous regions gathered to study. They would translate books from Greek, Persian, and Indian languages into Arabic, which preserved ancient knowledge that might otherwise have disappeared entirely.

These scholars investigated mathematics, astronomy, and medicine, and they composed original books that communicated their discoveries. One of them, the mathematician al-Khwarizmi, wrote an influential book about solving equations, and the word algebra originates from its Arabic title.

Eventually, papermaking spread to Spain and then across Europe, and today people around the world use paper every day, frequently without recognizing how much they owe to the papermakers and scholars of Abbasid Baghdad. Their remarkable achievements demonstrate how an inexpensive invention can revolutionize education, communication, and intellectual exchange.
